subject: Anthropology
title: Witchcraft and Social Control
description: A quick, practical guide to Witchcraft and Social Control.

hook.text: Fear of being accused of witchcraft keeps people generous and modest. Invisible threats enforce visible norms.

buildup.text: Witchcraft beliefs function as a form of social control, discouraging antisocial behavior through fear of accusation.

discovery.text: Evans-Pritchard showed that Azande witchcraft beliefs explain misfortune and regulate tensions in communities.

twist.text: Accusations target those who deviate. The greedy, the proud, and the envious face suspicion. Conformity keeps you safe.

climax.text: Witchcraft beliefs show that social control needs no police. Belief itself can enforce norms and punish deviance.

punchline.text: You don't need a prison when belief is the guard.

quiz.question: How do witchcraft beliefs function as social control?
options: Fear of accusation discourages deviance and enforces norms

details.summary: Witchcraft accusations function as political mechanisms in many societies — identifying and punishing those who violate social norms, accumulate too much wealth, or provoke jealousy. Witchcraft beliefs regulate behavior by threatening supernatural punishment for antisocial conduct.
details.whyItMatters: Witchcraft is not mere superstition but a political technology that enforces social conformity and manages tensions in communities without formal law enforcement. It reveals how supernatural beliefs serve concrete political functions.
takeaways: Witchcraft accusations enforce social norms and manage community tensions
Accusations target those who violate sharing norms or provoke jealousy
Supernatural beliefs serve concrete political and social functions

faq.question: How did Evans-Pritchard analyze witchcraft among the Azande?
faq.answer: Evans-Pritchard showed that Azande witchcraft beliefs formed a coherent logical system. Witchcraft explained misfortune — why this person got sick now, not just the biological cause.

faq.question: Who typically gets accused of witchcraft?
faq.answer: Accusations often target people who provoke social tension — the unusually wealthy, the antisocial, or those who refuse reciprocal obligations. In many African societies, witchcraft accusations function as leveling mechanisms that discourage individual accumulation at the community's expense.
